q: Where may a flexible compression joint NOT be placed at a manhole?
o: Embedded inside the manhole base
Within 0.3 m of the manhole wall
On the inlet pipe
On the outlet pipe
ref: 1999 Revised National Plumbing Code of the Philippines, Chapter 12 / Chapter 2 definitions
n: Manhole inlets and outlets get flexible joints close to the wall so settlement does not crack the pipe, but a joint cast into the base cannot flex.

q: What is the minimum size of a building sewer?
o: 100 mm (4 in)
150 mm (6 in)
75 mm (3 in)
200 mm (8 in)
ref: 1999 Revised National Plumbing Code of the Philippines, Chapter 12 / Chapter 2 definitions
n: Above that minimum, the sewer is sized from the total fixture units it drains.

q: What does a standard private sewage disposal system consist of?
o: A cesspool that takes raw sewage
A holding tank emptied into a storm drain
A septic tank whose effluent goes to a leaching field or seepage pit
A privy vault under an outhouse
ref: 1999 Revised National Plumbing Code of the Philippines, Chapter 12 / Chapter 2 definitions
n: The septic tank settles and digests solids, and the clarified effluent soaks into the soil.

q: Who must approve a cleanout placed inside a manhole?
o: The building owner
The city engineer's surveyor
The contractor's foreman
The Administrative Authority
ref: 1999 Revised National Plumbing Code of the Philippines, Chapter 12 / Chapter 2 definitions
n: The Administrative Authority (Plumbing Official) decides whether a manhole may serve as the cleanout point.

q: Where a sewer cannot be reached and soil will not take effluent, what may the Administrative Authority allow?
o: An approved watertight sewage holding tank
A cesspool with open joints
Discharge into a roadside canal
Discharge into a storm drain
ref: 1999 Revised National Plumbing Code of the Philippines, Chapter 12 / Chapter 2 definitions
n: A holding tank stores all sewage until a truck empties it. Nothing is released to the ground.

q: What is a seepage pit?
o: A watertight tank that stores sewage until pumped out
A loosely lined pit that lets septic tank effluent soak into the ground
A pit under a privy that holds excrement
A sump that collects storm water from a basement
ref: 1999 Revised National Plumbing Code of the Philippines, Chapter 12 / Chapter 2 definitions
n: The lining holds the pit open while effluent seeps through its sides and bottom.

q: Along how much of the building sewer, from the building drain, is no cleanout required?
o: The first 0.6 m
The first 15 m
The first 3.0 m
The whole length
ref: 1999 Revised National Plumbing Code of the Philippines, Chapter 12 / Chapter 2 definitions
n: Past 3.0 m, cleanouts are needed so the sewer can be rodded. They are extended to finished grade.

q: Where must rain and surface water NOT be discharged?
o: Into a storm drain
Into a dry well
Into a rain-harvesting cistern
Into the sanitary (excreta) drainage system
ref: 1999 Revised National Plumbing Code of the Philippines, Chapter 12 / Chapter 2 definitions
n: Storm water floods sanitary sewers and treatment plants, so the two systems are kept separate.

q: What must be done to an abandoned septic tank or sewage compartment?
o: Pump out the sewage and fill it with earth, sand, gravel or concrete
Seal the lid and leave it as it is
Connect it to the storm drain
Leave it open to air out
ref: 1999 Revised National Plumbing Code of the Philippines, Chapter 12 / Chapter 2 definitions
n: An empty tank can collapse or trap a person. Filling it removes both risks.

q: Where site conditions prevent a 2% slope, what is the minimum slope for a building sewer of 102 mm to 152.4 mm?
o: 20 mm per m (2%)
10 mm per m (1%)
5 mm per m (0.5%)
2 mm per m (0.2%)
ref: 1999 Revised National Plumbing Code of the Philippines, Chapter 12 / Chapter 2 definitions
n: Smaller sewers stay at 2%. Sewers 203 mm and larger may drop to 5 mm per m (0.5%).

q: When must a building connect to the public sewer?
o: Only when the septic tank fails
Only for buildings over three storeys
When a public sewer is available in the street fronting the lot
Only when the owner applies for it
ref: 1999 Revised National Plumbing Code of the Philippines, Chapter 12 / Chapter 2 definitions
n: Where a public sewer fronts the lot, connecting is mandatory and a private disposal system is not allowed.

q: How are pipes connected at a manhole's inlet and outlet?
o: With rigid cement-mortar joints
With threaded couplings
With lead-caulked joints
With flexible compression joints within 0.3 m of the manhole
ref: 1999 Revised National Plumbing Code of the Philippines, Chapter 12 / Chapter 2 definitions
n: Manholes and pipes settle differently. Flexible joints close to the wall keep the pipe from shearing.

q: What is the size of a building sewer based on?
o: The total fixture units it drains
The floor area of the building
The number of storeys
The length of the lot frontage
ref: 1999 Revised National Plumbing Code of the Philippines, Chapter 12 / Chapter 2 definitions
n: Each fixture is given a fixture-unit value. The total sets the pipe size from the code table.

q: What is a privy vault?
o: The tank of a flush water closet
The pit beneath a privy that receives excrement
The first compartment of a septic tank
A locked cabinet for cleaning supplies
ref: 1999 Revised National Plumbing Code of the Philippines, Chapter 12 / Chapter 2 definitions
n: A privy is an outhouse; its vault is the pit below. Privies are used only where there is no water-carried system.

q: How is a cleanout under concrete or asphalt paving kept accessible?
o: By marking it with paint on the paving
By leaving a hole in the paving
With a strong yard box with a hinged cover, or a flush cover with a countersunk nut
By burying it with a note on the plans
ref: 1999 Revised National Plumbing Code of the Philippines, Chapter 12 / Chapter 2 definitions
n: Paving over a cleanout makes it useless. A box or flush cover keeps it reachable and safe to walk on.

q: May a food-waste grinder discharge into a private sewage disposal system such as a septic tank?
o: Yes, if the tank is doubled in size
Yes, for single-family houses only
Yes, if a grease trap is added
No, it is not allowed
ref: 1999 Revised National Plumbing Code of the Philippines, Chapter 12 / Chapter 2 definitions
n: Ground food adds solids and grease that fill the tank fast and clog the leaching field.

q: What is a cesspool?
o: A non-watertight pit that receives raw sewage and lets it seep out
A watertight tank that digests solids
A loosely lined pit that takes septic tank effluent
A tank that stores sewage until pumped out
ref: 1999 Revised National Plumbing Code of the Philippines, Chapter 12 / Chapter 2 definitions
n: A cesspool leaks untreated sewage into the soil. It is not allowed for new work.

q: How far from the building must a building sewer be laid, and how deep at least?
o: 0.30 m from the wall, and at least 0.60 m deep
0.60 m from the wall, and at least 0.30 m below finished grade
1.50 m from the wall, and at least 1.0 m deep
Right against the footing, at any depth
ref: 1999 Revised National Plumbing Code of the Philippines, Chapter 12 / Chapter 2 definitions
n: The distance protects the foundation, and the cover protects the pipe.

q: Under the plumbing code, what is unlawful to put into a sewer or private disposal system?
o: Waste water from kitchen sinks
Waste from water closets
Any material that could damage or clog the system
Water from lavatories
ref: 1999 Revised National Plumbing Code of the Philippines, Chapter 12 / Chapter 2 definitions
n: Solvents, oils, rags and building debris damage pipes and treatment. Fixtures' normal waste is what the system is for.

q: Where must an abandoned building sewer be plugged or capped?
o: At the building wall
At the public sewer main
Anywhere along its length
Within 1.50 m of the property line
ref: 1999 Revised National Plumbing Code of the Philippines, Chapter 12 / Chapter 2 definitions
n: Capping near the property line isolates the old line from the public sewer.

q: What is the standard slope of a building sewer?
o: 20 mm per m (2%)
10 mm per m (1%)
5 mm per m (0.5%)
40 mm per m (4%)
ref: 1999 Revised National Plumbing Code of the Philippines, Chapter 12 / Chapter 2 definitions
n: At 2%, sewage flows fast enough to carry solids. Lower slopes are allowed only for larger pipes when site conditions demand it.

q: What must every building with plumbing fixtures be connected to?
o: The nearest storm drain
An approved public or private sewage disposal system
A roadside canal
A dry well
ref: 1999 Revised National Plumbing Code of the Philippines, Chapter 12 / Chapter 2 definitions
n: Sewage must go either to a public sewer or, where none is available, to an approved private system.

q: What is the maximum distance between manholes on a building sewer?
ref: 1999 Revised National Plumbing Code of the Philippines, Chapter 12 / Chapter 2 definitions
n: Sewer rods reach about 45 m from each end, so manholes are placed at most 91 m apart.

q: Where does the building sewer begin?
o: At the base of the soil stack
At the property line
At the public sewer main
0.60 m outside the building wall
ref: 1999 Revised National Plumbing Code of the Philippines, Chapter 12 / Chapter 2 definitions
n: The building drain runs inside and to 0.60 m outside the wall. The building sewer continues from there.

q: What is a privy?
o: An outhouse for the deposit of excrement
A private bathroom inside a house
A tank for flushing a water closet
A fixture for washing the body
ref: 1999 Revised National Plumbing Code of the Philippines, Chapter 12 / Chapter 2 definitions
n: Privies have no water-carried drainage. They are used in places with no sewer or water supply.

q: In which direction must a sewer cleanout open?
o: Against the direction of flow
In the direction of flow, or at a right angle to it
Straight down
Toward the nearest wall
ref: 1999 Revised National Plumbing Code of the Philippines, Chapter 12 / Chapter 2 definitions
n: The cleanout must let a rod be pushed downstream, the way the blockage will go.

q: What may NOT be connected to a building sewer that leads to the public sewer?
o: Waste from water closets
Waste from kitchen sinks
Effluent from cesspools, septic tanks, seepage pits or underdrains
Waste from floor drains
ref: 1999 Revised National Plumbing Code of the Philippines, Chapter 12 / Chapter 2 definitions
n: Once a public sewer is used, private disposal systems are abandoned, not linked to it.

q: What is a septic tank?
o: A loosely lined pit that lets effluent soak away
A non-watertight pit for raw sewage
A tank that stores sewage until pumped out
A watertight tank that settles and digests sewage solids
ref: 1999 Revised National Plumbing Code of the Philippines, Chapter 12 / Chapter 2 definitions
n: Solids settle as sludge and digest, scum floats, and the clear effluent flows on to the soil absorption system.

q: What must a building sewer be laid on?
o: A concrete cradle or firm bed
Loose fill straight from the excavation
Wooden blocks at each joint
Nothing; it may hang between joints
ref: 1999 Revised National Plumbing Code of the Philippines, Chapter 12 / Chapter 2 definitions
n: A continuous firm bed keeps the pipe at grade and stops it from sagging or cracking.

q: Under the plumbing code, when is a public sewer considered NOT available to a proposed building?
o: When it is more than 15 m away
When it is more than 62 m away
When it is more than 150 m away
When it is on the other side of the street
ref: 1999 Revised National Plumbing Code of the Philippines, Chapter 12 / Chapter 2 definitions
n: Beyond 62 m, a private disposal system may be used instead.
